newsitem.title: UK: Support for Britain's royals slides - poll.
newsitem.headline: Support for Britain's royals slides - poll.

text.p: Support among Britons for the royal family has fallen below 50 percent for the first time, said a poll published in the Guardian on Tuesday.
The poll, conducted by ICM, showed only 48 percent of Britons felt the country would be worse off without the royal family, a fall from 70 percent three years ago.
Thirty percent said the country would be better off without the royals, compared with just 13 percent 10 years ago.

The royal family has stumbled in public opinion over recent years because of a spate of divorces and public admissions of affairs by current heir-to-the-throne Prince Charles and his former wife, Princess Diana.
The latest twist centres on Diana's apparent new romance with millionaire film producer Dodi Fayed, son of controversial Harrods department store boss Mohammed Al Fayed.
The Guardian said the poll showed people aged over 65 were the only group to produce a clear majority that believed Britain would be worse off without the royal family.
The poll showed growing support for Prince Charles, son of Queen Elizabeth, to succeed her as monarch, with 55 percent saying he should take the throne compared with 44 percent a year ago.
Charles has admitted a long-standing affair with Camilla Parker-Bowles, who has now divorced her husband.
But more than three quarters of those polled rejected the idea of Parker-Bowles becoming queen, the Guardian said.

Around 55 percent believed that members of the royal family, government ministers and members of parliament were not bound to resign if they were having an affair, the poll showed. Forty percent felt it warranted a resignation.
Foreign Secretary Robin Cook announced earlier this month that he was leaving his wife Margaret to be with Gaynor Regan, who has been his parliamentary aide for the past five years.
The Labour government has backed Cook over the decision and he has not resigned despite fierce criticism from the opposition Conservative Party.
